title: Professionalization of Nursing, Nursing Philosophies, Metaparadigm and Overview of the Nursing Process
introduction: Professionalism defines how nurses deliver quality care anchored in respect, advocacy, responsibility, and lifelong self-reflection. Grounded in personal nursing philosophies and the four unifying metaparadigm concepts—human beings, environment, health, and nursing practice—the five-step nursing process provides the systematic, dynamic framework for critical thinking and individualized clinical care.
learningOutcomes: 1.1 Define professionalism in nursing, differentiate its three core components (cognitive, attitudinal, psychomotor), and identify real-world professional standards and soft skills.
1.2 Explain the meaning, ontological/epistemic/ethical claims, and lifelong development of a personal nursing philosophy.
1.3 Describe the four core concepts of the nursing metaparadigm (human beings, environment, health, and nursing practice) and how they interact holistically.
1.4 Trace the historical evolution of the nursing process from Lydia Hall (1955) through Yura and Walsh (1967), ANA Standards (1973, 1991), and NANDA (1974).
1.5 Explain the five overlapping phases of the nursing process, distinguishing subjective from objective data and outlining reasons client goals may go unmet.

content.heading: Professionalism in Nursing: Components, Applications, and Core Soft Skills
content.body: In nursing, professionalism means delivering quality patient care while honouring respect, advocacy, responsibility, clear communication, and continuous self-reflection for personal and professional growth. According to the Iranian Journal of Nursing and Midwifery Research (IJNMR), nursing professionalism spans three equally vital components: (1) Cognitive—continually learning professional conduct and applying expanding knowledge to prioritize and make sound clinical decisions; (2) Attitudinal—holding values and attitudes aligned with professional standards and organizational goals, including flexibility and constructive compromise; and (3) Psychomotor—advancing beyond clinical procedures to build management capability, understand professional commitments, and practise self-discipline and self-directed learning. Guided by the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) code of professional standards, nurses demonstrate professionalism in seven real-world areas: Care Comes First (listening, clear information, informed decisions, refusing gifts for preferential treatment), Individual Treatment (respecting unique values and beliefs), Respect Dignity (safeguarding privacy, never disclosing unauthorized data, preserving anonymity in coursework/research), Work Together (team cooperation and mutual respect), High Standards of Care (punctuality, recognizing scope limits, asking for help), Honesty and Integrity (never plagiarizing, maintaining an accurate CV), and Uphold Reputation (recognizing actions outside work carry consequences). Professionalism cultivates five core soft skills: Conflict Resolution (de-escalating issues while respecting all parties), Ethical Thinking (value-based judgments placing patients first), Adaptability (combining new evidence and guidelines to improve solutions), Leadership (founded on communication, detail, respect, and resourcefulness), and Collaboration—developed continuously through workplace reflection and advanced nursing education.

content.heading: Nursing Philosophies and Their Clinical Significance
content.body: Fawcett and DeSanto-Madeya (2013) define a philosophy of nursing as a statement encompassing ontological claims (about phenomena central to the discipline), epistemic claims (about how those phenomena come to be known), and ethical claims (about what members of the discipline value). Philosophies articulate foundational beliefs and ethical knowledge that guide nurses in safeguarding privacy, upholding dignity, and navigating emotionally demanding care where healing relationships are not always reciprocal. Building a personal nursing philosophy is an ongoing journey of self-discovery reflecting personal and professional values, goals, ethics, and calling. As Marchuk (2014) notes, articulating a philosophy helps nurses recognize how thinking drives clinical actions, maximizes knowledge application, and can even inspire theory creation. Beyond everyday habits, a nursing philosophy includes an abstract theoretical lens that prepares clinicians to respond ethically when unexpected dilemmas arise. Because it is a practiced art shaped organically by both clinical encounters and life experiences, a nursing philosophy is never 'finished'—nurses benefit from writing it down and revising it as they grow professionally.

content.heading: Major Concepts in Nursing: The Four Metaparadigm Concepts
content.body: A metaparadigm provides the overarching theoretical structure governing how a discipline functions. Across diverse nursing theories, four interactive metaparadigm concepts establish holistic care: (1) Human Beings—viewed as unique, dynamic, sentient, multidimensional open energy fields greater than and different from the sum of their parts, capable of abstract reasoning, creativity, empathy, and informed health choices; encompassing interrelated biological, psychological, spiritual, intellectual, and sociocultural dimensions across individuals, families, and communities; (2) Environment—the landscape and geography of human social experience across space, time, and quality (personal, social, national, global), including cultural beliefs, values, mores, customs, and physical, psychosocial, historical, political, and economic forces interacting mutually with the human energy field; (3) Health—a dynamic, contextual, relational synthesis of wellness (lived congruence between possibilities and realities grounded in caring) and illness (lived experience of loss or dysfunction mediated by caring), shaped by stress, coping, and person-environment interaction; and (4) Nursing Practice—an academic discipline and practice profession uniting nursing science (theory, research, logical analysis) and nursing art (creative therapeutic interventions) guided by human freedom, choice, responsibility, critical thinking, and clinical judgment.

content.heading: Historical Perspectives of the Nursing Process
content.body: The nursing process is the universal framework for delivering professional, individualized, holistic care across health promotion, health protection, and disease prevention—providing 'the basis for critical thinking in nursing' (Alfaro-LeFavre, 1998). Its formal evolution spanned four decades: Lydia Hall first described nursing as a 'process' in a 1955 journal article (gaining widespread adoption in the late 1960s); Johnson (1959), Orlando (1961), and Wiedenbach (1963) conceptualized a three-step nursing process (assessment, planning, evaluation); Yura and Walsh expanded this to four steps (Assessing, Planning, Implementing, Evaluating) in their 1967 book The Nursing Process; the American Nurses Association (ANA) published eight Standards of Practice in 1973 incorporating nursing diagnosis; although Fry (1953) first coined the term 'nursing diagnosis', Gebbie and Lavin formally added nursing diagnosis as a distinct step in 1974 following the first meeting of the group that became the North American Nursing Diagnosis Association (NANDA); and in 1991, the ANA revised its standards to incorporate outcome identification explicitly within planning, yielding the five modern steps: Assessment, Diagnosis, Outcome Identification/Planning, Implementation, and Evaluation.

content.heading: The Five Phases of the Nursing Process
content.body: Although sequential in logic, the five phases of the nursing process are non-linear and continually overlap: (1) Assessment—systematic, dynamic collection and analysis of holistic physiological, psychological, sociocultural, spiritual, economic, and lifestyle data forming the client database. Subjective data capture the client's verbalized perceptions, feelings, and concerns primarily via therapeutic interview (e.g., 'I have had pains in my legs for three days'), whereas Objective data are observable, measurable findings gathered through physical examination and diagnostic tests (e.g., vital signs, bowel sounds, shuffling gait); validating subjective against objective data prevents omissions, misunderstandings, and faulty inferences. (2) Diagnosis—NANDA-I (2018–2020) defines nursing diagnosis as a clinical judgment concerning a human response to health conditions/life processes, or vulnerability for that response, by an individual, family, group, or community; it guides intervention selection for which the nurse is accountable (Carroll-Johnson, 1990). (3) Outcome Identification / Planning—formulating measurable, achievable short- and long-range goals and a written plan of care accessible to the health team. (4) Implementation—executing planned nursing actions while assessing the client before (baseline), during, and after interventions (detecting positive or negative responses), applying psychomotor, interpersonal, and critical thinking skills alongside reporting and documentation. (5) Evaluation—determining whether goals are met, partially met, or not met and deciding whether to terminate, maintain, or modify care; unmet or partially met goals commonly stem from incomplete initial assessment data, unrealistic goals, overly optimistic time frames, or inappropriate nursing interventions.

inTextQuestions.question: Which theorist first referred to nursing as a 'process' in 1955, and who expanded the nursing process to four steps in 1967?
inTextQuestions.answer: Lydia Hall first referred to nursing as a 'process' in 1955; Yura and Walsh expanded it to four steps (Assessing, Planning, Implementing, Evaluating) in 1967.

inTextQuestions.question: What are the four basic concepts that make up the nursing metaparadigm?
inTextQuestions.answer: Human Beings (Person), Environment, Health, and Nursing Practice.

inTextQuestions.question: Why is data validation considered a critical step during nursing assessment?
inTextQuestions.answer: Validating subjective data against objective findings avoids omissions, prevents misunderstandings, and prevents incorrect clinical inferences and conclusions.

inTextQuestions.question: Does the evaluation phase precede the documentation phase in nursing care? Explain.
inTextQuestions.answer: False. Evaluation typically follows the implementation and documentation of previously rendered nursing care so the nurse can judge whether expected outcomes were achieved.

saqs.question: Differentiate the cognitive, attitudinal, and psychomotor components of nursing professionalism and list five soft skills attributed to professionalism.
saqs.answer: Cognitive professionalism focuses on continuous learning of professional conduct and applying knowledge to prioritize and make decisions; Attitudinal involves aligning attitudes/ideas with standards and organizational goals with flexibility; Psychomotor covers sharpening clinical and management skills, self-discipline, and self-learning. Five soft skills: conflict resolution, ethical thinking, adaptability, leadership, and collaboration.

saqs.question: Define a philosophy of nursing according to Fawcett and DeSanto-Madeya (2013) and explain why a personal nursing philosophy is never 'finished'.
saqs.answer: A philosophy of nursing is a statement encompassing ontological claims (central phenomena of interest), epistemic claims (how those phenomena come to be known), and ethical claims (what discipline members value). It is never finished because it is a practiced art shaped organically and continuously by daily clinical situations, evolving knowledge, and personal life experiences.

saqs.question: Explain each of the four nursing metaparadigm concepts and how wellness and illness are conceptualized under Health.
saqs.answer: Human Beings are holistic, multidimensional open energy fields greater than the sum of their parts; Environment is the physical, social, cultural, political, and economic landscape interacting mutually with the human field; Nursing Practice unites scientific knowledge and creative therapeutic art guided by critical thinking; Health is a dynamic synthesis of wellness (lived congruence between possibilities and realities grounded in caring) and illness (lived loss or dysfunction mediated by caring).

saqs.question: Trace the major historical milestones in the development of the five-step nursing process between 1953 and 1991.
saqs.answer: 1953: Fry first used 'nursing diagnosis'. 1955: Lydia Hall called nursing a 'process'. 1959–1963: Johnson, Orlando, and Wiedenbach described a 3-step process (assessment, planning, evaluation). 1967: Yura and Walsh identified 4 steps (adding implementation). 1973: ANA published 8 Standards of Practice including diagnosis. 1974: Gebbie and Lavin established nursing diagnosis as a distinct step after NANDA's 1973 founding meeting. 1991: ANA added outcome identification explicitly within planning.

saqs.question: Distinguish subjective from objective assessment data with two examples each, and state four common reasons client goals may be unmet or partially met during evaluation.
saqs.answer: Subjective data are client-verbalized feelings, perceptions, and concerns gathered via interview (e.g., 'I have leg pain for three days', 'I wake up after two hours of sleep'). Objective data are observable, measurable findings from exams/tests (e.g., BP 130/76, slow shuffling gait). Four reasons goals go unmet: incomplete initial assessment data, unrealistic goals/outcomes, overly optimistic time frames, and inappropriate nursing interventions.
